paper_b.title: Orthogonal Matching Pursuit: Recursive Function Approximation with Applications to Wavelet Decomposition

metadata.description: Both papers attack the sparse-representation problem in overcomplete dictionaries but from substantially different theoretical machinery: Chen-Donoho-Saunders (BP) frames it as global convex optimization (l1 minimization solved by linear programming / interior-point), while Pati-Rezaiifar-Krishnaprasad (OMP) keeps the greedy MP framework and refines it with per-step orthogonalization. Paper A explicitly cites OMP (AP264.3) as a competing greedy baseline and exhibits a counterexample (ExP264.7) where OMP fails; paper B predates BP and does not consider l1-minimization. The shared object is the dictionary / sparse representation problem; the methods are competing frameworks for solving it.

matches.explanation: Both define a 'dictionary' as a (possibly overcomplete) collection of waveforms / unit-norm vectors used to decompose signals. Paper A works in discrete-time R^n; paper B works in an abstract Hilbert space and additionally introduces the closed span V and its orthogonal complement W. Same mathematical object up to ambient-space generality and the explicit unit-norm normalization in B; both papers are PDF-fallback so we trust the matching name and type.

Same problem statement: given an overcomplete dictionary and a signal, find a coefficient vector representing the signal. Both flag non-uniqueness and target sparsity. Paper B further specifies the optimal-N-term approximation as the orthogonal projection onto the span of the chosen atoms (captured separately by DP265.2).

Paper B factors the sparse-representation problem into a separate definition (DP265.2, optimal N-term approximation) plus the problem (ProbP265.1). The optimality criterion in DP265.2 (R_N f in V_N^perp, i.e. f_N is the orthogonal projection) corresponds to the implicit best-N-atom criterion behind paper A's overcomplete representation problem; cross-type (problem vs definition) match recorded for completeness.

Both nodes describe Matching Pursuit (Mallat & Zhang 1993/1992) and are tagged origin=external in their respective graphs with the same citation. Pseudocode (greedy selection of the atom most correlated with the residual, scalar coefficient, residual update) is identical. Paper B includes the slackness parameter alpha; paper A omits it but the underlying algorithm is the same.

AP264.3 is paper A's one-paragraph description of OMP, marked origin=external with citation 'Pati, Rezaiifar, Krishnaprasad 1993; Davis, Mallat, Zhang 1994'. AP265.2 is the original OMP definition by paper B. Same algorithm: greedy atom selection followed by least-squares re-projection so the residual is orthogonal to the entire span of selected atoms. Paper B provides the full pseudocode and the auxiliary update machinery (DP265.3, PrP265.2-5, ASP265.*); paper A only needs the high-level statement to compare against BP.

Composite L2-vs-L1 entry per v2 rule 1: paper A's OMP node is a single-sentence description with no algorithm_step children, while paper B decomposes OMP into eight algorithm steps (initialize, compute inner products, select, stopping check, reorder, solve auxiliary system, update coefficients/model/residual, iterate). The step decomposition is paper B's contribution; emitting it as a many-to-many companion to the L1 match (AP264.3 ↔ AP265.2) keeps that contribution visible in the alignment.

Cluster of wavelet/wavelet-packet/stationary-wavelet dictionaries on the BP side vs paper B's single Mexican-hat affine wavelet dictionary used in its experiments. All are translation/dilation families of a mother wavelet, and DP264.5 (Haar) plus DP264.8 (stationary wavelets) are closest in spirit to DP265.4 (continuous-affine Mexican-hat frame). Tagged analogous because the specific mother wavelets and discretizations differ; serves as the example-dictionary correspondence between the two papers.

Both are remarks motivating better-than-MP algorithms by pointing out MP's failure modes. RP264.2 ('MP myopia') argues MP makes wrong early choices in non-orthogonal dictionaries and spends iterations correcting them, with TwinSine/DeVore-Temlyakov/Chen examples. RP265.1 ('Suboptimality of MP at finite N') argues that MP only orthogonalises against the last selected atom, so f_N is generally not the best N-term approximation. The flavour differs (BP uses MP's myopia to motivate l1; OMP uses it to motivate full re-orthogonalization), so analogous rather than exact.

Both are toy counterexamples designed to expose a greedy-pursuit failure. ExP264.7 ('Chen's OMP counterexample') is constructed precisely to defeat OMP, showing it picks the wrong atoms first; ExP265.1 (R^2 illustration) shows MP failing in two dimensions while OMP succeeds in two iterations. They play structurally parallel motivational roles inside their respective papers - one motivating BP over OMP, the other motivating OMP over MP - so the match is conceptually analogous rather than mathematically equivalent.

Secondary parallel: ExP264.6 (DeVore-Temlyakov MP counterexample, dictionary of n+1 atoms making MP error decay only as O(1/sqrt(m))) plays a similar didactic role to paper B's R^2 toy example - both are constructed to expose deficiencies of the greedy framework that the new method fixes. Low confidence because the constructions and quantitative claims differ substantially.

Both papers devote attention to making their algorithms practical by avoiding explicit dense linear-algebra costs. RP264.4 substitutes fast implicit Phi, Phi^T plus conjugate gradients (LSQR) for sparse-LP solvers in BP-Interior. Paper B's PrP265.4 (recursive update of residual inner products) and PrP265.5 (block-recursive Gram inversion) play the same computational-shortcut role for OMP. Different objects (LP central equation vs Gram matrix) but parallel in spirit; cross-type (remark vs proposition) recorded.

EP264.1 (signal decomposition equation s = sum alpha_gamma phi_gamma plus residual) has no separate equation node in paper B, but the same identity is implicit in DP265.1 / ProbP265.1 / AP265.1. Recorded as none because no atomic equation node exists on the B side; not a meaningful contribution-level gap.

Basis Pursuit itself - min ||alpha||_1 subject to Phi alpha = s - is the central paper-original contribution of paper A and has no counterpart in paper B, which predates BP and never considers l1 minimization. This is the primary axis of the CF relation.
Basis Pursuit Denoising (l1-regularised least squares) is paper-original to A. Paper B does not address noisy data or any quadratic-plus-l1 functional.
BP-to-LP translation (the explicit dictionary recasting BP as a standard-form LP) is paper-original to A. Paper B uses no LP machinery.
BPDN's universal threshold lambda_p = sigma sqrt(2 log p) is a paper-original noise-aware tuning rule of A; B has no analogue (no noise model, no threshold parameter beyond the OMP stopping epsilon).
Central interior-point step equation (ADA^T + delta^2 I) Delta y = ... is paper-original to A's BP-Interior algorithm; no counterpart in B.
Theorem 'Soft thresholding equals BPDN in orthogonal basis' is paper-original to A. The result fundamentally requires the l1 penalty introduced by BPDN and has no OMP analogue.
BP-Simplex (simplex method applied to BP's LP equivalent) is paper-original to A and entirely tied to the LP formulation of BP.
BP-Interior (primal-dual log-barrier interior-point solver for BP) is paper-original to A. Paper B has no continuous-optimization solver.
BPDN-Interior is paper-original to A and specific to the noisy-data BPDN formulation.

Stationary wavelet dictionary is a paper-original construction of A (translation-invariant overcomplete wavelet frame). It is partially absorbed into the wavelet-dictionary cluster match above with DP265.4, but its specific contribution (full circulant invariance, O(n log n) size) is paper-A-original; recorded none as well to flag the contribution explicitly.
Carbon synthetic-signal example is paper-original to A and showcases BP's exact-recovery behaviour on a six-atom mixture; no analogue in B.
TwinSine super-resolution example is paper-original to A; B does not address super-resolution.
FM-Cosine cosine-packet example is paper-original to A.
Gong example is paper-original to A and used to demonstrate BPDN at SNR=1; no counterpart in B.
WernerSorrows example is paper-original to A and contrasts BP against entropy-based BOB selection; no counterpart in B.
HeaviSine / multiscale-edges example is paper-original to A and addresses CWT-maxima alignment, outside B's scope.
Blocks / TV-denoising example is paper-original to A and tied to the BPDN+heaviside framing.
Cusp / jump+wave example is paper-original to A.
Remark on MOF sparsity failure is paper-original to A and concerns the l2-pseudoinverse method, outside B's scope.
Fast-implicit-algorithms remark catalogues FFT/wavelet/wavelet-packet operator costs used by A's BP-Interior; not present in B.
BP-Interior improves on MOF: paper-original observation about the specific BP solver lineage. No analogue in B.
BOB-initialization for BP-Simplex: paper-original to A. No analogue in B (B has no LP / no BOB).
Recommended numerical settings for BP / BPDN solvers: paper-original to A's implementation discussion. No analogue in B.

Auxiliary decomposition of the newly selected atom (x_{k+1} = sum b_n^k x_n + gamma_k) is paper-original to B and underpins the OMP coefficient update. Paper A's OMP description (AP264.3) does not expose this internal object.
Order-k to order-(k+1) coefficient update rule for OMP is paper-original to B; not surfaced in A's compressed OMP description.
OMP residual update and energy identity is paper-original to B; A does not discuss OMP's energy decrement.

OMP convergence theorem (residuals converge to projection onto closed span; f_N equals best N-term projection) is paper-original to B. Paper A relies on this property implicitly when describing OMP but does not state it as a result.
Finite-dictionary termination of OMP in <= |D| steps is paper-original to B and not present in A.
Conjecture that OMP outperforms MP on highly redundant dictionaries is paper-original to B and concerns greedy-vs-greedy comparison; A's narrative is BP-vs-greedy.
Assumption that the OMP stopping threshold epsilon > 0 ensures non-singularity of A_k is paper-original to B (regularity condition for the block-recursive Gram inversion). No analogue in A.
Wavelet experiment Example I (351-atom Mexican-hat dictionary, OMP vs MP iteration / FLOP comparison) is paper-original to B and specific to the OMP-vs-MP narrative.
Wavelet experiment Example II (3-atom signal, OMP recovers in three iterations) is paper-original to B.

Dirac dictionary (standard orthogonal basis 1_{t=gamma}) is a concrete dictionary instance introduced by A to support its examples (TwinSine, Donoho-Huo). Paper B uses only the Mexican-hat affine wavelet dictionary (DP265.4), so this paper-A definition has no B counterpart.
Heaviside dictionary (step waveforms 1_{t>=gamma}) is a paper-A concrete dictionary used for TV-denoising and the Blocks example. No counterpart in B.
Fourier dictionary (cosine and sine atoms; l-fold overcomplete variant) is a paper-A concrete dictionary; B does not use Fourier atoms.

Analysis vs synthesis distinction (synthesis s = Phi alpha vs analysis tilde-alpha = Phi^T s, distinct in the overcomplete case) is paper A's framing definition. Paper B works only with the synthesis side and never explicitly draws this dichotomy, so the definition has no B counterpart.
Proof of OMP convergence theorem (TP265.1) is paper-original to B. Paper A has no proof of OMP's properties (it only describes the algorithm at a high level).
